title: Λέχους σῆμα
titleEn: The Secret of the Bed — Odyssey 23.183–287
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus answers Penelope's order to move the bed by asking who could have moved it, and tells her how he built it: he walled and roofed a chamber round an olive that grew in the enclosure, trimmed its trunk into a bedpost and built the bed from it, so that no man could shift the bed unless someone had cut the tree at its base. Penelope's knees give way at the proof. She runs to him, throws her arms round his neck, and asks him not to be angry that she did not welcome him at once: she has always feared deceivers, and the only people who have ever seen the couch are the two of them and one attendant. Her words stir his tears, and the poem compares her joy to that of shipwrecked swimmers reaching land. Athena holds back the Dawn to lengthen the night. When Odysseus says that a great labour still lies ahead, Penelope asks to hear it, and he tells what the soul of Teiresias foretold: a journey inland with an oar until a traveller takes it for a winnowing-shovel, a sacrifice to Poseidon, and a mild death in a sleek old age with his people prosperous around him. Penelope answers that if the gods grant a better old age, there is hope of escape from evils.

sentences.t: ὦ γύναι, ἦ μάλα τοῦτο ἔπος θυμαλγὲς ἔειπες·
sentences.tr: ō gynai, ē mala touto epos thymalges eeipes·
sentences.l: “Wife, truly very this word, heart-paining, you have spoken;
sentences.i: “Wife, you have spoken a word that pains my heart deeply;
sentences.n: Odysseus answers; the narrator introduced the speech in the last line of the previous part, so the opening quotation mark falls here. He is replying to Penelope's order, at the end of that part, to have the solid bed spread outside the chamber. ὦ γύναι is 'wife', the vocative of γυνή. ἦ μάλα is 'truly, very'. ἔπος θυμαλγές is 'a word that pains the heart': θυμαλγές joins θυμός 'heart' to ἄλγος 'pain' and agrees with ἔπος. ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον 'say' with the epic doubled ε- (Attic εἶπες).

sentences.t: τίς δέ μοι ἄλλοσε θῆκε λέχος;
sentences.tr: tis de moi allose thēke lechos;
sentences.l: But who, for me, has put the bed elsewhere?
sentences.i: But who has put my bed somewhere else?
sentences.n: He takes her order to mean that the bed has been moved. ἄλλοσε is 'to another place': the suffix -σε marks direction, as -δε does in οἶκόνδε 'homeward'. θῆκε is the aorist of τίθημι 'put', without the augment that Attic would add (ἔθηκε); μοι is a dative of interest, 'for me'. λέχος is 'bed', the word Odysseus uses for it in his account (184–204); Penelope, who said λέχος in the previous part (177, 179), speaks of it here as εὐνή 'couch' (226, 257). The Greek question mark ends the unit in the middle of line 184.

sentences.t:
χαλεπὸν δέ κεν εἴη
καὶ μάλ’ ἐπισταμένῳ, ὅτε μὴ θεὸς αὐτὸς ἐπελθὼν
ῥηϊδίως ἐθέλων θείη ἄλλῃ ἐνὶ χώρῃ.
sentences.tr:
chalepon de ken eiē
kai mal’ epistamenōi, hote mē theos autos epelthōn
rhēïdiōs ethelōn theiē allēi eni chōrēi.
sentences.l:
And hard it would be
even for one very skilled, unless a god himself, coming,
with ease, being willing, should set it in another place.
sentences.i: It would be hard even for a very skilful man, unless a god came himself and, if he wished, moved it with ease to another place.
sentences.n: χαλεπὸν δέ κεν εἴη is a potential optative (κεν = ἄν), 'it would be hard'; χαλεπόν is 'hard' of a task, not 'harsh'. ἐπισταμένῳ is the dative participle of ἐπίσταμαι 'know how, be skilled', 'for one who is skilled'; καὶ μάλα strengthens it, 'even a very ...'. ὅτε μή is 'unless'. θείη is the aorist optative of τίθημι, the verb of θῆκε in the first half of line 184 (the unit before), and ἐπελθών is 'coming upon' it. ῥηϊδίως is the epic form of ῥᾳδίως 'easily', and ἐθέλων 'being willing'. The point is that only a god could move the bed; a man could not.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρῶν δ’ οὔ κέν τις ζωὸς βροτός, οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἡβῶν,
ῥεῖα μετοχλίσσειεν, ἐπεὶ μέγα σῆμα τέτυκται
ἐν λέχει ἀσκητῷ·
sentences.tr:
andrōn d’ ou ken tis zōos brotos, oude mal’ hēbōn,
rheia metochlisseien, epei mega sēma tetyktai
en lechei askētōi·
sentences.i: No living mortal man, not even one in the full strength of youth, could easily move it, for a great sign has been wrought into the artfully fashioned bed;
sentences.n: ἀνδρῶν is a partitive genitive: 'of men, any living mortal'. κέν with the optative μετοχλίσσειεν makes a potential, 'would shift'; the verb is built on μοχλός 'lever', so it means 'move out of its place'. ἡβῶν is the participle of ἡβάω 'be in the prime of youth', from ἥβη 'youth'. ῥεῖα is 'easily'. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω 'make', 'has been wrought'. ἀσκητῷ 'artfully fashioned' comes from ἀσκέω 'work with art', the verb of ἀσκήσας at 198. The sign is explained from line 190 on.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ἐγὼ κάμον οὐδέ τις ἄλλος.
sentences.tr: to d’ egō kamon oude tis allos.
sentences.l: and that I toiled at, and not anyone else.
sentences.i: and I was the one who toiled at it, and no one else.
sentences.n: τό is the pronoun 'that' (in Homer the article is a pronoun), the object of κάμον. κάμον is the aorist of κάμνω 'toil, labour at', without the augment Attic would add (ἔκαμον). The claim that he alone worked on it is what makes the sign private to the two of them.

sentences.t:
θάμνος ἔφυ τανύφυλλος ἐλαίης ἕρκεος ἐντός,
ἀκμηνὸς θαλέθων·
sentences.tr:
thamnos ephy tanyphyllos elaiēs herkeos entos,
akmēnos thalethōn·
sentences.l:
A bush grew, long-leaved, of an olive, inside the enclosure,
full-grown, flourishing;
sentences.i: Inside the enclosure there grew a long-leaved bush of olive, full-grown and flourishing;
sentences.n: θάμνος is 'bush, shrub'; ἔφυ is the aorist of φύω 'grow' in its intransitive sense. τανύφυλλος is 'long-leaved' (τανυ- 'long' with φύλλον 'leaf'), and ἐλαίης is the genitive of ἐλαία 'olive' in Ionic -ης (Attic ἐλαίας). ἕρκεος ἐντός is 'inside the enclosure': ἕρκος is a fence, or the fenced yard it makes. ἀκμηνός is a rare word, traditionally glossed 'full-grown'; θαλέθων is the participle of θαλέθω 'flourish', from the root of θάλλω.

sentences.t: πάχετος δ’ ἦν ἠΰτε κίων.
sentences.tr: pachetos d’ ēn ēÿte kiōn.
sentences.l: and thick it was, like a pillar.
sentences.i: and it was as thick as a pillar.
sentences.n: πάχετος is an epic adjective 'thick', beside Attic παχύς. ἦν is the imperfect of εἰμί. ἠΰτε is 'like, as' and introduces a comparison; κίων is 'pillar'. The unit begins in the middle of line 191, after the · of the unit before, and ends with the line.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐγὼ ἀμφιβαλὼν θάλαμον δέμον, ὄφρ’ ἐτέλεσσα,
πυκνῇσιν λιθάδεσσι, καὶ εὖ καθύπερθεν ἔρεψα,
κολλητὰς δ’ ἐπέθηκα θύρας, πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ egō amphibalōn thalamon demon, ophr’ etelessa,
pyknēisin lithadessi, kai eu kathyperthen erepsa,
kollētas d’ epethēka thyras, pykinōs araruias.
sentences.l:
And around it, casting, a chamber I built, until I finished it,
with close-set stones, and well on top I roofed it,
and close-joined doors I set on, closely fitted.
sentences.i: I built a chamber round it, with close-set stones, until I had finished it, and roofed it well, and set close-joined doors on it, tightly fitted.
sentences.n: τῷ is the pronoun 'it', the dative that ἀμφιβαλών 'putting round' takes: he built the walls round the olive. θάλαμος is an inner room, 'chamber'. δέμον is the aorist of δέμω 'build', without augment, and ὄφρ’ ἐτέλεσσα 'until I finished' (ἐτέλεσσα is ἐτέλεσα with doubled σ) ends both line 192 and line 199. λιθάδεσσι is the dative plural of λιθάς 'stone' in -εσσι; καθύπερθεν is 'on top'; ἔρεψα is the aorist of ἐρέφω 'roof'. κολλητάς is 'close-joined' (κολλάω 'glue, join'), and ἀραρυίας is the feminine accusative plural of the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit'.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπέκοψα κόμην τανυφύλλου ἐλαίης,
κορμὸν δ’ ἐκ ῥίζης προταμὼν ἀμφέξεσα χαλκῷ
εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως, καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνα,
ἑρμῖν’ ἀσκήσας, τέτρηνα δὲ πάντα τερέτρῳ.
sentences.tr:
kai tot’ epeit’ apekopsa komēn tanyphyllou elaiēs,
kormon d’ ek rhizēs protamōn amphexesa chalkōi
eu kai epistamenōs, kai epi stathmēn ithyna,
hermin’ askēsas, tetrēna de panta teretrōi.
sentences.l:
And then thereupon I lopped off the foliage of the long-leaved olive,
and the trunk, from the root cutting forward, I trimmed all round with bronze
well and skilfully, and to the line I made it straight,
having fashioned a bedpost, and I bored it all with an auger.
sentences.i: Then I lopped off the foliage of the long-leaved olive, cut the trunk forward from the root and trimmed it all round with the bronze, well and skilfully, and made it true to the line, fashioning a bedpost, and bored it all through with an auger.
sentences.n: κόμη is 'hair', here the leafy crown of the tree. κορμὸν δ’ ἐκ ῥίζης προταμών is 'cutting the trunk (forward) from the root', that is, trimming it starting at the root; the Greek does not say that the trunk is cut free of the root. ἀμφέξεσα is the aorist of ἀμφιξέω 'trim all round', and the bronze is the cutting tool. ἐπισταμένως is 'skilfully', the adverb of the participle in 185. στάθμη is a carpenter's line, and ἴθυνα the aorist of ἰθύνω 'make straight'. ἑρμῖν’ is ἑρμῖνα, 'bedpost'; ἀσκήσας is the aorist participle of ἀσκέω, as ἀσκητῷ in 189. τέτρηνα is the aorist of τετραίνω 'bore', and τερέτρῳ the dative of τέρετρον 'auger'. This is the longest sentence of the description, four lines.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἀρχόμενος λέχος ἔξεον, ὄφρ’ ἐτέλεσσα,
δαιδάλλων χρυσῷ τε καὶ ἀργύρῳ ἠδ’ ἐλέφαντι·
sentences.tr:
ek de tou archomenos lechos exeon, ophr’ etelessa,
daidallōn chrysōi te kai argyrōi ēd’ elephanti·
sentences.l:
And starting from this I planed the bed, until I had finished it,
adorning it with gold and with silver and with ivory;
sentences.i: Starting from this I planed the bed into shape until it was finished, adorning it with gold and silver and ivory;
sentences.n: ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἀρχόμενος is 'and beginning from this', τοῦ being the pronoun 'it', the post just shaped. ἔξεον is the imperfect of ξέω 'plane, smooth', so 'I was planing'. ὄφρ’ ἐτέλεσσα repeats the end of line 192. δαιδάλλων is 'adorning with cunning work'; χρυσῷ, ἀργύρῳ and ἐλέφαντι are datives of material, joined by τε καί and ἠδέ, an epic 'and'.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἐτάνυσσα ἱμάντα βοὸς φοίνικι φαεινόν.
sentences.tr: ek d’ etanyssa himanta boos phoiniki phaeinon.
sentences.l: and I stretched out a strap of oxhide, shining with crimson.
sentences.i: and I stretched across it a strap of oxhide, shining with crimson.
sentences.n: ἐκ δ’ ἐτάνυσσα is tmesis: the preverb ἐκ stands apart from the verb, which is ἐκτανύω 'stretch out, stretch taut'. ἱμάς is a strap or thong (accusative ἱμάντα), here of ox-hide (βοός), and it is the webbing of the bed. φοίνικι is the dative of φοῖνιξ 'crimson' (the dye), and φαεινόν 'shining' agrees with ἱμάντα.

sentences.t: οὕτω τοι τόδε σῆμα πιφαύσκομαι·
sentences.tr: houtō toi tode sēma piphauskomai·
sentences.l: Thus to you this sign I make known;
sentences.i: That is the sign I make known to you;
sentences.n: οὕτω is 'thus'. τοι is the enclitic 'to you' (σοί). σῆμα is the sign announced at 188; it is the same word as the 'signs' of the test in the previous part. πιφαύσκομαι is the present middle of πιφαύσκω 'make known, show'. The · ends the unit in the middle of line 202.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι οἶδα,
ἤ μοι ἔτ’ ἔμπεδόν ἐστι, γύναι, λέχος, ἦέ τις ἤδη
ἀνδρῶν ἄλλοσε θῆκε, ταμὼν ὕπο πυθμέν’ ἐλαίης.
sentences.tr:
oude ti oida,
ē moi et’ empedon esti, gynai, lechos, ēe tis ēdē
andrōn allose thēke, tamōn hypo pythmen’ elaiēs.
sentences.l:
and I do not know at all
whether still for me it stands firm, wife, the bed, or whether some one already
of men has put it elsewhere, cutting beneath the base of the olive.”
sentences.i: and I do not know whether it still stands firm for me, wife, the bed, or whether some man has already put it elsewhere by cutting under the base of the olive.”
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι οἶδα is 'and I do not know at all' (τι is adverbial). ἤ … ἦέ is 'whether … or'. ἔμπεδον is 'firm, in place'. θῆκε is the verb of 184, and ἀνδρῶν again partitive, 'one of men'. ταμὼν ὕπο is tmesis for ὑποταμών 'cutting under', with ὕπο accented because it follows its word; πυθμήν is the base of the tree. The question of 184 returns here in the one form that could be true: if the olive was cut through at its base, the bed was moved. The closing quotation mark falls at the end of the line, which ends the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῆς δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ,
σήματ’ ἀναγνούσῃ τά οἱ ἔμπεδα πέφραδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tēs d’ autou lyto gounata kai philon ētor,
sēmat’ anagnousēi ta hoi empeda pephrad’ Odysseus·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and then her knees were loosed, and her dear heart,
in her who recognised the signs which Odysseus had told her, sure ones.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and her knees gave way at once, and her heart too, as she recognised the sure signs which Odysseus had told her;
sentences.n: Narration. The first line is the same line as 4.703 and keeps its English: ὣς φάτο is 'So he spoke', τῆς is the pronoun 'her', and λύτο is an aorist middle of λύω, passive in sense (unaugmented), 'were loosed'; the knees and the heart giving way is the formula for a collapse of feeling. αὐτοῦ is 'there, on the spot'. The second line is the same as 19.250, where Penelope also recognises tokens. ἀναγνούσῃ is the feminine dative aorist participle of ἀναγιγνώσκω 'recognise, know again', ἔμπεδα 'sure, firm' (as ἔμπεδον at 203) agrees with σήματα, and πέφραδ’ is the reduplicated aorist of φράζω 'point out, tell'.

sentences.t:
δακρύσασα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἰθὺς δράμεν, ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρας
δειρῇ βάλλ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ, κάρη δ’ ἔκυσ’ ἠδὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
dakrysasa d’ epeit’ ithys dramen, amphi de cheiras
deirēi ball’ Odysēï, karē d’ ekys’ ēde prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And having shed tears, then straight she ran, and around her hands
to the neck she threw, to Odysseus, and kissed his head and spoke to him:
sentences.i: Then, weeping, she ran straight to him and threw her arms round the neck of Odysseus, and kissed his head, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: δακρύσασα is the aorist participle of δακρύω 'shed tears'. δράμεν is the aorist of τρέχω without augment (Attic ἔδραμεν), and ἰθύς 'straight'. ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρας … βάλλ’ is tmesis for 'threw her arms round'; βάλλ’ is the imperfect βάλλε with the vowel elided. δειρῇ is the dative of δειρή 'neck' (Attic δέρη), and Ὀδυσῆϊ the dative of the person whose neck it is, a form of Ὀδυσσεύς with a single σ. ἔκυσ’ is the aorist of κυνέω 'kiss', κάρη the epic 'head', and προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to'. The · ends the unit: the speech follows.

sentences.t:
μή μοι, Ὀδυσσεῦ, σκύζευ, ἐπεὶ τά περ ἄλλα μάλιστα
ἀνθρώπων πέπνυσο·
sentences.tr:
mē moi, Odysseu, skyzeu, epei ta per alla malista
anthrōpōn pepnyso·
sentences.l:
“Do not, to me, Odysseus, be angry, since in the other things most of all
of men you are prudent;
sentences.i: “Do not be angry with me, Odysseus, for in everything else you are the most prudent of men;
sentences.n: Penelope answers. μή μοι … σκύζευ is a prohibition with the present imperative of σκύζομαι 'be angry', 'do not be angry with me'. Ὀδυσσεῦ is the vocative. τά περ ἄλλα is an accusative of respect, 'in all other matters', περ strengthening it. πέπνυσο is the second person singular of the perfect of a verb related to πεπνυμένος 'prudent', the epithet of Telemachus; the perfect has present sense, 'you are prudent'. ἀνθρώπων is a partitive genitive with the superlative μάλιστα, 'of men'.

sentences.t:
θεοὶ δ’ ὤπαζον ὀϊζύν,
οἳ νῶϊν ἀγάσαντο παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι μένοντε
ἥβης ταρπῆναι καὶ γήραος οὐδὸν ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
theoi d’ ōpazon oïzyn,
hoi nōïn agasanto par’ allēloisi menonte
hēbēs tarpēnai kai gēraos oudon hikesthai.
sentences.l:
but the gods gave us distress,
who resented us two, beside one another staying,
that we should take our fill of youth and reach the threshold of old age.
sentences.i: but the gods gave us distress; they resented that we two, staying together, should take our fill of youth and come to the threshold of old age.
sentences.n: ὤπαζον is the imperfect of ὀπάζω 'give, bestow'. ὀϊζύς is 'distress'. οἵ is the relative 'who'; νῶϊν is the dative dual 'to us two'; μένοντε, 'we two staying', is a dual participle in the form shared by nominative and accusative, going with the unspoken 'we two' that are the subject of ταρπῆναι rather than agreeing in case with νῶϊν. ἀγάσαντο is the aorist middle of ἀγάομαι 'be resentful of, begrudge'. ἀλλήλοισι is the dative plural 'one another'. ταρπῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of τέρπω, 'be satisfied, take one's fill of', with the genitive ἥβης 'youth'. γήραος is the epic genitive of γῆρας 'old age', and οὐδός is 'threshold': 'to reach the threshold of old age' is a figure for 'to grow old'. ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι 'come to'. Line 211 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the short second syllable of νῶϊν is counted long, in the second foot, before ἀγάσαντο.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ μὴ νῦν μοι τόδε χώεο μηδὲ νεμέσσα,
οὕνεκά σ’ οὐ τὸ πρῶτον, ἐπεὶ ἴδον, ὧδ’ ἀγάπησα.
sentences.tr:
autar mē nyn moi tode chōeo mēde nemessa,
houneka s’ ou to prōton, epei idon, hōd’ agapēsa.
sentences.l:
But do not now be incensed at this with me, nor take offence,
that I did not, at first, when I saw you, thus greet you warmly.
sentences.i: But do not now be incensed with me for this, nor hold it against me, that I did not greet you lovingly like this when I first saw you.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but'. μὴ … χώεο μηδὲ νεμέσσα are two prohibitions: χώεο is the imperative of χώομαι 'be incensed, be angry' (a second verb of anger beside σκύζευ), and νεμέσσα the imperative of νεμεσσάω 'feel resentment'. οὕνεκα is 'because, that'. τὸ πρῶτον is 'at first'; ἴδον is the aorist of ὁράω without augment (Attic εἶδον); ἀγάπησα is the aorist of ἀγαπάω, 'welcome with affection', and ὧδε 'in this way', that is, as lovingly as she greets him now.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ γάρ μοι θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισιν
ἐρρίγει μή τίς με βροτῶν ἀπάφοιτο ἔπεσσιν
ἐλθών·
sentences.tr:
aiei gar moi thymos eni stēthessi philoisin
errigei mē tis me brotōn apaphoito epessin
elthōn·
sentences.i: For the heart in my breast always shuddered, afraid that some mortal would come and deceive me with his words;
sentences.n: αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί. θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισιν is 'my heart in my dear breast', στήθεσσι being the dative plural of στῆθος in -εσσι and φίλοισιν a dative in -οισιν. ἐρρίγει is the pluperfect of ῥιγέω 'shudder, shrink in fear', used like an imperfect. μή with the optative ἀπάφοιτο, the aorist middle optative of ἀπαφίσκω 'deceive', gives 'lest … deceive me'; τις βροτῶν is 'some one of mortals'. ἐλθών 'coming' belongs to the deceiver. The · ends the unit in the middle of line 217.

sentences.t: πολλοὶ γὰρ κακὰ κέρδεα βουλεύουσιν.
sentences.tr: polloi gar kaka kerdea bouleuousin.
sentences.l: for many evil cunning-ways devise.
sentences.i: for there are many who devise evil, cunning ways.
sentences.n: πολλοί is 'many' (understood: many men), and γάρ gives the reason for her fear. κέρδος is 'gain, profit', and in the plural often 'cunning schemes, wiles'; κακά 'evil' agrees with κέρδεα, which is the uncontracted plural (Attic κέρδη). The house rendering 'cunning ways' keeps the word in step with κέρδεα οἶδεν. βουλεύουσιν is 'they plan, devise'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα,
ἀνδρὶ παρ’ ἀλλοδαπῷ ἐμίγη φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ,
εἰ ᾔδη ὅ μιν αὖτις ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
ἀξέμεναι οἶκόνδε φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἔμελλον.
sentences.tr:
oude ken Argeiē Helenē, Dios ekgegauia,
andri par’ allodapōi emigē philotēti kai eunēi,
ei ēidē ho min autis arēïoi huies Achaiōn
axemenai oikonde philēn es patrid’ emellon.
sentences.l:
Not even Argive Helen, sprung of Zeus,
with a foreign man would have been mingled in love and in bed,
if she had known that her again the warlike sons of the Achaeans
were going to lead home to her dear fatherland.
sentences.i: Not even Argive Helen, the daughter sprung from Zeus, would have lain in love with a foreign man, if she had known that the warlike sons of the Achaeans were going to take her home again to her dear fatherland.
sentences.n: Penelope argues from Helen's case. οὐδέ κεν … ἐμίγη is a contrary-to-fact main clause: κεν with the aorist indicative, 'would not have been mingled' (Attic οὐκ ἄν). Ἀργείη is the Ionic feminine of Ἀργεῖος 'Argive', and Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα the feminine perfect participle of ἐκγίγνομαι, 'having sprung from Zeus'. ἀλλοδαπῷ is the dative of ἀλλοδαπός 'from another land'. ἐμίγη is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι 'mix'. ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα, 'had known', and ὅ is ὅτι 'that'. ἀρήϊοι is 'warlike'. ἀξέμεναι is the future infinitive of ἄγω in -έμεναι, 'were going to lead'. οἶκόνδε is 'homeward' (-δε).

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἦ τοι ῥέξαι θεὸς ὤρορεν ἔργον ἀεικές·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ē toi rhexai theos ōroren ergon aeikes·
sentences.l: But her, to do, a god urged an unseemly deed;
sentences.i: It was a god, indeed, who urged her to do an unseemly deed;
sentences.n: τὴν is the pronoun 'her' (in Homer the article is a pronoun), and ἦ τοι 'verily, indeed'. ῥέξαι is the aorist infinitive of ῥέζω 'do'. ὤρορεν is the reduplicated aorist of ὄρνυμι 'rouse, urge on', the verb of ὦρσε at 231. ἀεικές is the neuter of ἀεικής 'unseemly, not fitting'. Penelope excuses Helen: a god, not Helen, made her act.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ ἄτην οὐ πρόσθεν ἑῷ ἐγκάτθετο θυμῷ
λυγρήν, ἐξ ἧς πρῶτα καὶ ἡμέας ἵκετο πένθος.
sentences.tr:
tēn d’ atēn ou prosthen heōi enkattheto thymōi
lygrēn, ex hēs prōta kai hēmeas hiketo penthos.
sentences.l:
but that bewilderment, not before in her own heart did she lay it,
grievous, from which first on us too came grief.
sentences.i: But she had not before taken that grievous bewilderment into her own heart, the bewilderment from which grief first came on us too.
sentences.n: ἄτη is the clouding of the mind, and the ruin that follows from it; 'bewilderment' names the state. τὴν … ἄτην … λυγρήν 'that grievous bewilderment' is the object of ἐγκάτθετο, the aorist middle of ἐγκατατίθημι 'lay up in', and οὐ πρόσθεν is 'not before'. ἑῷ is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν 'her own', not the relative. ἐξ ἧς is 'from which'; πρῶτα is 'first'; ἡμέας is the Ionic ἡμᾶς 'us'; ἵκετο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι without augment, 'came'. In Penelope's account Helen had not foreseen where her bewilderment would lead.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’, ἐπεὶ ἤδη σήματ’ ἀριφραδέα κατέλεξας
εὐνῆς ἡμετέρης, ἣν οὐ βροτὸς ἄλλος ὀπώπει,
sentences.tr:
nyn d’, epei ēdē sēmat’ ariphradea katelexas
eunēs hēmeterēs, hēn ou brotos allos opōpei,
sentences.l:
But now, since already signs very plain you have recounted
of our couch, which no other mortal had seen,
sentences.i: But now, since you have recounted the very plain signs of our couch, which no other mortal had seen,
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ is 'but now'; ἐπεὶ ἤδη 'since already'. σήματ’ ἀριφραδέα is 'very plain signs': ἀριφραδής is ἀρι- 'very' with the root of φράζω. κατέλεξας is the aorist of καταλέγω 'recount'. εὐνῆς ἡμετέρης is 'of our couch': εὐνή is 'couch'; Penelope uses it here for the bed itself, where Odysseus said λέχος (and she herself said λέχος in the previous part, 177, 179). ὀπώπει is the pluperfect of ὄπωπα 'have seen', so 'had seen'. This is the first of three units cut at the commas of one six-line sentence; the main verb comes at 230.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἶοι σύ τ’ ἐγώ τε καὶ ἀμφίπολος μία μούνη,
Ἀκτορίς, ἥν μοι δῶκε πατὴρ ἔτι δεῦρο κιούσῃ,
ἣ νῶϊν εἴρυτο θύρας πυκινοῦ θαλάμοιο,
sentences.tr:
all’ oioi sy t’ egō te kai amphipolos mia mounē,
Aktoris, hēn moi dōke patēr eti deuro kiousēi,
hē nōïn eiryto thyras pykinou thalamoio,
sentences.l:
but only you and I and one attendant, alone,
Actoris, whom to me gave my father when still coming here,
who for us two guarded the doors of the solid chamber,
sentences.i: but only you and I and one attendant alone, Actoris, whom my father gave me when I was still on my way here, who kept the doors of our solid chamber for us two,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ here is 'except': no mortal had seen the couch except these three. οἶοι is the nominative plural of οἶος 'alone, only', and σύ τ’ ἐγώ τε 'both you and I'. ἀμφίπολος μία μούνη is 'one attendant alone'. Ἀκτορίς is a woman's name. ἥν μοι δῶκε is 'whom my father gave to me', and ἔτι δεῦρο κιούσῃ is a dative participle of κίω, 'to me still coming here'. νῶϊν is the dative dual 'for us two'. εἴρυτο is a past tense of ἐρύομαι 'guard, keep'. πυκινοῦ θαλάμοιο has the genitive in -οιο (= -ου), 'of the solid chamber'. Line 229 is metrically irregular as transmitted, as 211 is: it scans only if the short second syllable of νῶϊν is counted long, in the second foot, before εἴρυτο.

sentences.t: πείθεις δή μευ θυμόν, ἀπηνέα περ μάλ’ ἐόντα.
sentences.tr: peitheis dē meu thymon, apēnea per mal’ eonta.
sentences.l: you persuade, indeed, my heart, though very unkind it is.”
sentences.i: you are persuading my heart, though it is very unkind.”
sentences.n: πείθεις is 'you persuade', δή 'indeed'. μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, 'my', with θυμόν. ἀπηνέα is the accusative of ἀπηνής 'unkind, harsh', and περ 'although' goes with ἐόντα, the participle of εἰμί (Attic ὄντα), agreeing with θυμόν. It is the charge that Telemachus made against her in the previous part, an unkind heart, and she admits that it is her own heart that has now been won. The closing quotation mark falls here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tōi d’ eti mallon hyph’ himeron ōrse gooio·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and in him all the more she stirred the longing for lament;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and all the more she stirred in him the longing to lament;
sentences.n: Narration. ὣς φάτο is 'So she spoke' (the same wording as for a man). This line repeats, with τῷ 'in him' for τῇ 'in her', 19.249. τῷ is the pronoun, and ἔτι μᾶλλον 'still more'. ὑφ’ … ὦρσε is tmesis for ὑπώρσε, from ὄρνυμι 'rouse'; ἵμερον is 'longing', and γόοιο the genitive of γόος 'lament' in -οιο.

sentences.t: κλαῖε δ’ ἔχων ἄλοχον θυμαρέα, κεδνὰ ἰδυῖαν.
sentences.tr: klaie d’ echōn alochon thymarea, kedna iduian.
sentences.l: and he wept, holding his wife, heart-fitting, the one wise and trusty.
sentences.i: and he wept as he held his wife, who suited his heart, trusty and wise.
sentences.n: κλαῖε is the imperfect of κλαίω 'weep', ἔχων 'holding'. θυμαρέα is the accusative of θυμαρής 'agreeable to the heart' (θυμός with the root of ἀραρίσκω 'fit'), so 'heart-fitting'. κεδνὰ ἰδυῖαν is the stock epithet of the wife, translated every time: ἰδυῖαν is the feminine accusative of the perfect participle of οἶδα, 'knowing', and κεδνά is 'trusty things', 'the one wise and trusty'. It closes the previous part too.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀσπάσιος γῆ νηχομένοισι φανήῃ,
ὧν τε Ποσειδάων εὐεργέα νῆ’ ἐνὶ πόντῳ
ῥαίσῃ, ἐπειγομένην ἀνέμῳ καὶ κύματι πηγῷ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an aspasios gē nēchomenoisi phanēēi,
hōn te Poseidaōn euergea nē’ eni pontōi
rhaisēi, epeigomenēn anemōi kai kymati pēgōi·
sentences.i: As when land appears, a welcome sight, to swimmers whose well-made ship Poseidon has shattered on the sea, driven on by wind and heavy wave;
sentences.n: A simile begins; it is completed at 239. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν is 'and as when', with the subjunctive φανήῃ 'appears' (general). ἀσπάσιος is 'welcome', of the land: 'a welcome sight'. γῆ is 'land', and νηχομένοισι the dative plural participle of νήχομαι 'swim'. ὧν τε is the genitive of the relative, 'whose', with epic τε. εὐεργέα is 'well-made'; νῆ’ is νῆα, the accusative of νηῦς 'ship'; ῥαίσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ῥαίω 'shatter'. ἐπειγομένην 'pressed, driven' agrees with the ship. πηγῷ is a rare epithet of the wave, ancient guesses 'massed, solid' (from πήγνυμι 'make firm') or 'strong'; the sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
παῦροι δ’ ἐξέφυγον πολιῆς ἁλὸς ἤπειρόνδε
νηχόμενοι, πολλὴ δὲ περὶ χροῒ τέτροφεν ἅλμη,
ἀσπάσιοι δ’ ἐπέβαν γαίης, κακότητα φυγόντες·
sentences.tr:
pauroi d’ exephygon poliēs halos ēpeironde
nēchomenoi, pollē de peri chroï tetrophen halmē,
aspasioi d’ epeban gaiēs, kakotēta phygontes·
sentences.i: and few escape from the grey sea to reach the mainland, swimming, with thick brine caked on their skin, and glad they set foot on the land, having escaped misfortune;
sentences.n: παῦροι is 'few'. ἐξέφυγον and ἐπέβαν are gnomic aorists: the simile tells what always happens, so the English uses the present. πολιῆς ἁλός is 'of the grey sea' (πολιός 'grey'), and ἤπειρόνδε is 'to the mainland' (-δε). τέτροφεν is the perfect of τρέφω in its rare sense 'thicken, cake', and ἅλμη is 'brine'; χροΐ is the dative of χρώς 'skin'. ἀσπάσιοι, said of the swimmers, is 'glad'. ἐπέβαν is the aorist of ἐπιβαίνω (3 pl., = ἐπέβησαν) with the genitive γαίης 'land'. κακότης is 'ill fortune, misfortune'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τῇ ἀσπαστὸς ἔην πόσις εἰσοροώσῃ,
δειρῆς δ’ οὔ πω πάμπαν ἀφίετο πήχεε λευκώ.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara tēi aspastos eēn posis eisoroōsēi,
deirēs d’ ou pō pampan aphieto pēchee leukō.
sentences.l:
so then to her welcome was her husband as she looked on him,
and from the neck not yet entirely were let go the two white arms.
sentences.i: so welcome was her husband to her as she looked at him, and her white arms were not yet quite loosed from his neck.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα returns from the simile: as land is to swimmers, so her husband is to her. ἀσπαστός is 'welcome' (here of a person), and ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). εἰσοροώσῃ is the uncontracted dative participle of εἰσοράω 'look at' (Attic εἰσορώσῃ). δειρῆς is the genitive of δειρή 'neck'. ἀφίετο is the imperfect passive of ἀφίημι 'let go'. πήχεε λευκώ is a dual, 'the two white arms'; the verb ἀφίετο is singular although its subject is dual. οὔ πω πάμπαν is 'not yet altogether'.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ὀδυρομένοισι φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
kai ny k’ odyromenoisi phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
ei mē ar’ all’ enoēse thea glaukōpis Athēnē.
sentences.l:
And now for them lamenting would have appeared rose-fingered Dawn,
if the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, had not then devised another thing.
sentences.i: And rose-fingered Dawn would have appeared on them as they lamented, if the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, had not thought of something else.
sentences.n: καί νύ κ’ is καὶ νύ κε. κε with the aorist φάνη makes a contrary-to-fact main clause, 'would have appeared', the condition being εἰ μὴ … ἐνόησε 'if she had not thought of'. ὀδυρομένοισι is the dative plural participle of ὀδύρομαι 'lament'. ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς is the stock epithet of Dawn, 'rose-fingered'. ἄλλ’ is ἄλλο 'another thing'. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is the goddess with her stock epithet. The next four lines say what she thought of.

sentences.t:
νύκτα μὲν ἐν περάτῃ δολιχὴν σχέθεν, Ἠῶ δ’ αὖτε
ῥύσατ’ ἐπ’ Ὠκεανῷ χρυσόθρονον, οὐδ’ ἔα ἵππους
ζεύγνυσθ’ ὠκύποδας, φάος ἀνθρώποισι φέροντας,
Λάμπον καὶ Φαέθονθ’, οἵ τ’ Ἠῶ πῶλοι ἄγουσι.
sentences.tr:
nykta men en peratēi dolichēn schethen, Ēō d’ aute
rhysat’ ep’ Ōkeanōi chrysothronon, oud’ ea hippous
zeugnysth’ ōkypodas, phaos anthrōpoisi pherontas,
Lampon kai Phaethonth’, hoi t’ Ēō pōloi agousi.
sentences.l:
Night at the far edge she held back long, and Dawn in turn
she kept at Oceanus, the golden-throned, and did not let her
yoke the swift-footed horses, bringing light to men,
Lampus and Phaethon, the colts which bring Dawn.
sentences.i: She held back long night at the far edge of the world, and kept golden-throned Dawn at Oceanus, and would not let her yoke her swift-footed horses, which bring light to men, Lampus and Phaethon, the colts that bring Dawn.
sentences.n: σχέθεν is the aorist of ἔχω 'hold, check' without augment (Attic ἔσχεν). ἐν περάτῃ is 'at the farthest limit' (πέρας 'limit'); the Greek does not say of what; the literal line keeps 'the far edge', and the free English spells it out as 'of the world'. μὲν … δ’ αὖτε sets the two actions side by side, Night kept long and Dawn kept back. ῥύσατ’ is the aorist middle of ῥύομαι, here 'draw back, hold back'; ἐπ’ Ὠκεανῷ is 'at Oceanus'; χρυσόθρονον is 'golden-throned' (an old alternative takes the second part from θρόνα 'embroidered flowers'). οὐδ’ ἔα is the imperfect of ἐάω 'allow'; ζεύγνυσθ’ is the middle infinitive of ζεύγνυμι 'yoke'. ὠκύποδας is 'swift-footed' (ὠκύς with πούς). Λάμπον and Φαέθονθ’ are the horses' names, accusatives in apposition to ἵππους; οἵ is the relative, the subject of ἄγουσι, and πῶλοι 'colts' stands in apposition to it. The sentence is four lines long and stops at the full stop.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ ἣν ἄλοχον προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ ar’ hēn alochon prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: And then indeed his own wife he addressed, many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles said to his own wife:
sentences.n: Narration introducing Odysseus's speech. καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ is 'and then indeed'. ἣν ἄλοχον is 'his own wife': ἥν is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, not the relative. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to, address'. πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς is the stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι, οὐ γάρ πω πάντων ἐπὶ πείρατ’ ἀέθλων
ἤλθομεν, ἀλλ’ ἔτ’ ὄπισθεν ἀμέτρητος πόνος ἔσται,
πολλὸς καὶ χαλεπός, τὸν ἐμὲ χρὴ πάντα τελέσσαι.
sentences.tr:
ō gynai, ou gar pō pantōn epi peirat’ aethlōn
ēlthomen, all’ et’ opisthen ametrētos ponos estai,
pollos kai chalepos, ton eme chrē panta telessai.
sentences.l:
“Wife, for not yet to the limits of all trials
have we come, but still behind there will be an unmeasured toil,
much and hard, which me it is necessary all to accomplish.
sentences.i: “Wife, we have not yet come to the limit of all our trials, but there will still be an unmeasured toil ahead, great and hard, which I must bring entirely to completion.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks. οὐ γάρ πω is 'for not yet'. πείρατα is the plural of πεῖραρ 'limit, end', and ἀέθλων the genitive of ἄεθλος, 'trial', here the labours of his journey. ἤλθομεν is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, 'we have come'. ὄπισθεν is 'behind', that is, still to come. ἀμέτρητος is 'unmeasured' (ἀ- with μετρέω). πολλός is the epic form of πολύς, and χαλεπός 'hard' (of a toil, as of a task). τὸν ἐμὲ χρὴ πάντα τελέσσαι is 'which I must accomplish in full': χρή takes the accusative and infinitive, and τελέσσαι is the aorist infinitive of τελέω with doubled σ.

sentences.t:
ὣς γάρ μοι ψυχὴ μαντεύσατο Τειρεσίαο
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε δὴ κατέβην δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
νόστον ἑταίροισιν διζήμενος ἠδ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
hōs gar moi psychē manteusato Teiresiao
ēmati tōi hote dē katebēn domon Aïdos eisō,
noston hetairoisin dizēmenos ēd’ emoi autōi.
sentences.l:
For so to me the soul of Teiresias prophesied
on that day when I went down to the house of Hades,
seeking a homecoming for my companions and for myself.
sentences.i: For so the soul of Teiresias prophesied to me on the day when I went down into the house of Hades, seeking a homecoming for my companions and for myself.
sentences.n: ὣς γάρ is 'for so'. ψυχή is the soul of the dead, and Τειρεσίαο the epic genitive of Τειρεσίας in -αο (Attic -ου). μαντεύσατο is the aorist middle of μαντεύομαι 'prophesy'. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε δή is 'on that day when', ἤματι the dative of ἦμαρ. κατέβην is 'I went down', and δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω 'into the house of Hades', εἴσω taking the accusative of the place entered. διζήμενος is 'seeking', and ἑταίροισιν, ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ are datives, 'for my companions, for myself'. νόστον is 'homecoming', the return to one's own country.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔρχευ, λέκτρονδ’ ἴομεν, γύναι, ὄφρα καὶ ἤδη
ὕπνῳ ὕπο γλυκερῷ ταρπώμεθα κοιμηθέντε.
sentences.tr:
all’ ercheu, lektrond’ iomen, gynai, ophra kai ēdē
hypnōi hypo glykerōi tarpōmetha koimēthente.
sentences.l:
But come, to bed let us go, wife, so that even now
under sweet sleep we may take our fill, we two having lain down.”
sentences.i: But come, wife, let us go to bed, so that even now we two may lie down and take our fill of sweet sleep.”
sentences.n: ἔρχευ is the imperative of ἔρχομαι 'come' (-ευ for -εο). λέκτρονδ’ is λέκτρονδε 'to bed' (λέκτρον is the same family as λέχος; -δε marks direction). ἴομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive, 'let us go' (Attic ἴωμεν). ὄφρα with the subjunctive ταρπώμεθα gives purpose; ταρπώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive of the verb of ταρπῆναι at 212, 'take our fill', and ὕπνῳ ὕπο γλυκερῷ is 'under sweet sleep', ὕπο accented because it follows its noun. κοιμηθέντε is the nominative dual aorist passive participle of κοιμάω, 'we two having lain down'. The closing quotation mark falls here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The formula that brings Penelope in to answer her husband; the same line stands at 285 and in an earlier part, and its English is the same each time. τὸν is the pronoun 'him' (in Homer the article is a pronoun), αὖτε is 'in turn, again', and προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον 'speak to, address', a reply verb distinct from ἠμείβετο 'answered'. περίφρων 'circumspect' is her stock epithet.

sentences.t:
εὐνὴ μὲν δή σοί γε τότ’ ἔσσεται ὁππότε θυμῷ
σῷ ἐθέλῃς, ἐπεὶ ἄρ σε θεοὶ ποίησαν ἱκέσθαι
οἶκον ἐϋκτίμενον καὶ σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
eunē men dē soi ge tot’ essetai hoppote thymōi
sōi ethelēis, epei ar se theoi poiēsan hikesthai
oikon eÿktimenon kai sēn es patrida gaian·
sentences.i: “You will have your couch, then, whenever you wish it in your own heart, since the gods have brought you to your well-built home and your own native land;
sentences.n: Penelope answers. εὐνὴ μὲν δή σοί γε τότ’ ἔσσεται is 'a couch will indeed be yours then' (ἔσσεται = ἔσται), and ὁππότε is 'whenever' (Attic ὁπότε), with the subjunctive ἐθέλῃς; σῷ is the possessive 'your'. ἐπεὶ ἄρ is 'since indeed'. ποίησαν is the aorist of ποιέω, which with the infinitive ἱκέσθαι means 'caused you to come'. Line 259 is the same as a line of an earlier part, and its English is kept: ἐϋκτίμενον is 'well-built', and πατρίδα γαῖαν 'fatherland'. The · ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἐφράσθης καί τοι θεὸς ἔμβαλε θυμῷ,
εἴπ’ ἄγε μοι τὸν ἄεθλον, ἐπεὶ καὶ ὄπισθεν, ὀΐω,
πεύσομαι, αὐτίκα δ’ ἐστὶ δαήμεναι οὔ τι χέρειον.
sentences.tr:
all’ epei ephrasthēs kai toi theos embale thymōi,
eip’ age moi ton aethlon, epei kai opisthen, oïō,
peusomai, autika d’ esti daēmenai ou ti chereion.
sentences.l:
But since you noticed, and to you a god cast it into your heart,
tell me, come, of that trial, since also afterwards, I think,
I shall learn, and at once to learn is not at all worse.”
sentences.i: But since you have noticed it, and a god has put it into your heart, tell me, come now, about the trial, since I think I shall learn of it afterwards in any case, and it is no worse to learn it at once.”
sentences.n: The first line is the same as a line of an earlier part and keeps its English. ἐφράσθης is the aorist of φράζομαι 'notice'; καί τοι θεὸς ἔμβαλε θυμῷ is 'and a god put it into your heart', τοι being σοι and ἔμβαλε the aorist of ἐμβάλλω 'cast in'. εἴπ’ ἄγε μοι is 'tell me, come'. τὸν ἄεθλον is 'that trial', τόν a demonstrative pointing to the trial of 248–250. ὄπισθεν is 'afterwards' (compare 249), and ὀΐω 'I think'. πεύσομαι is the future of πυνθάνομαι 'learn by asking'. δαήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of the verb of ἐδάην, 'to learn', in -ήμεναι. χέρειον is 'worse'. The closing quotation mark falls here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: The formula that brings Odysseus in to reply. τὴν is the pronoun 'her', ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering', and προσέφη 'addressed'. πολύμητις 'of many wiles' is his stock epithet, here in the line that has stood in earlier parts, whose English is kept. The line ends in ·, and the speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
δαιμονίη, τί τ’ ἄρ’ αὖ με μάλ’ ὀτρύνουσα κελεύεις
εἰπέμεν;
sentences.tr:
daimoniē, ti t’ ar’ au me mal’ otrynousa keleueis
eipemen;
sentences.l:
“Strange woman, why then again do you urge me so hard and bid
me tell?
sentences.i: “Strange woman, why do you press me so hard again, and tell me to say it?
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. δαιμονίη is 'strange woman', the feminine of δαιμόνιε; the address can be affectionate or chiding, and its force is uncertain, so the translation stays literal. τί τ’ ἄρ’ αὖ is 'why then again' (τε is the epic particle). μάλ’ ὀτρύνουσα is 'urging hard' and κελεύεις 'you bid'. εἰπέμεν is the infinitive in -έμεν (Attic εἰπεῖν). The Greek question mark ends the unit in the middle of line 265.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω.
sentences.tr: autar egō mythēsomai oud’ epikeusō.
sentences.l: But I will tell it, and I will not hide it.
sentences.i: But I will tell it, and I will hide nothing.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but'. μυθήσομαι is the future of μυθέομαι 'tell'. ἐπικεύσω is the aorist subjunctive of ἐπικεύθω 'hide', used with future sense (a short-vowel subjunctive). The two verbs together, tell and not hide, promise that nothing will be held back.

sentences.t: οὐ μέν τοι θυμὸς κεχαρήσεται·
sentences.tr: ou men toi thymos kecharēsetai·
sentences.l: Indeed not will your heart rejoice;
sentences.i: Your heart will not rejoice at it;
sentences.n: οὐ μέν is 'indeed not', and τοι is σοι, 'to you', which English gives as 'your heart'. κεχαρήσεται is a reduplicated future of χαίρω 'rejoice'. θυμός is 'heart'. The · ends the unit in the middle of line 266.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτὸς
χαίρω, ἐπεὶ μάλα πολλὰ βροτῶν ἐπὶ ἄστε’ ἄνωγεν
ἐλθεῖν, ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔχοντ’ εὐῆρες ἐρετμόν,
sentences.tr:
oude gar autos
chairō, epei mala polla brotōn epi aste’ anōgen
elthein, en cheiressin echont’ euēres eretmon,
sentences.l:
for not even I myself
rejoice, since to very many towns of mortals he bade
me go, holding in my hands a well-fitted oar,
sentences.i: for I do not rejoice in it myself, since he told me to go to a great many towns of men, with a well-fitted oar in my hands,
sentences.n: οὐδὲ γάρ is 'for … not even'; αὐτός 'I myself'. ἄνωγεν is the perfect ἄνωγα 'bid' with the sense of a past tense here: 'he bade'. The subject is not named, but it is the soul of Teiresias of line 251. μάλα πολλά is 'very many', agreeing with ἄστε’, which is ἄστεα 'towns'; βροτῶν ἐπὶ ἄστε’ is 'to the towns of mortals'. ἐλθεῖν is the aorist infinitive of ἔρχομαι, and ἔχοντ’ the accusative participle of ἔχω agreeing with the unspoken 'me'. ἐν χείρεσσιν is the dative plural in -εσσιν, 'in my hands'. εὐῆρες 'well-fitted' comes from ἀραρίσκω 'fit', and ἐρετμόν is 'oar'.

sentences.t:
εἰς ὅ κε τοὺς ἀφίκωμαι οἳ οὐκ ἴσασι θάλασσαν
ἀνέρες, οὐδέ θ’ ἅλεσσι μεμιγμένον εἶδαρ ἔδουσιν·
sentences.tr:
eis ho ke tous aphikōmai hoi ouk isasi thalassan
aneres, oude th’ halessi memigmenon eidar edousin·
sentences.l:
until I reach those who do not know the sea,
men who not even food mixed with salt eat;
sentences.i: until I come to men who know nothing of the sea and eat no food mixed with salt;
sentences.n: εἰς ὅ κε is 'until' (κε = ἄν), with the subjunctive ἀφίκωμαι 'I reach'. τοὺς … οἳ οὐκ ἴσασι θάλασσαν is 'those who do not know the sea', ἴσασι being the third plural of οἶδα. ἀνέρες is ἄνδρες 'men', in apposition. ἅλεσσι is the dative plural of ἅλς in its sense 'salt' (the same noun means 'sea'); μεμιγμένον is the perfect passive participle of μίγνυμι, 'mixed', and εἶδαρ is 'food'. ἔδουσιν is the third plural of ἔδω 'eat'. This passage is a repeat, with 'I' for 'you', of a passage in an earlier part and keeps its English. The · ends the unit.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γ’ ἴσασι νέας φοινικοπαρῄους,
οὐδ’ εὐήρε’ ἐρετμά, τά τε πτερὰ νηυσὶ πέλονται.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara toi g’ isasi neas phoinikoparēious,
oud’ euēre’ eretma, ta te ptera nēusi pelontai.
sentences.l:
nor indeed do they know ships crimson-cheeked,
nor well-fitted oars, which wings for ships are.
sentences.i: nor do they know ships with crimson cheeks, or well-fitted oars, which serve ships as wings.
sentences.n: These two lines are the same as two lines of an earlier part (apart from a spelling), and their English is kept. οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γ’ is 'nor indeed they'. νέας is the epic accusative plural of νηῦς 'ship'. φοινικοπαρῄους 'crimson-cheeked' is built on παρῃά 'cheek', the side of a ship's bow. ἐρετμά is the plural of ἐρετμόν, and τά τε πτερὰ νηυσὶ πέλονται is 'which are wings for ships', τά the relative, νηυσί the dative plural of νηῦς.

sentences.t: σῆμα δέ μοι τόδ’ ἔειπεν ἀριφραδές, οὐδέ σε κεύσω·
sentences.tr: sēma de moi tod’ eeipen ariphrades, oude se keusō·
sentences.l: And a sign to me this he told, very plain, nor will I hide it from you;
sentences.i: He told me this very plain sign, and I will not hide it from you:
sentences.n: σῆμα … ἔειπεν is 'he told a sign'; ἔειπεν is the epic aorist of εἶπον. ἀριφραδές is 'very plain'. κεύσω is the aorist subjunctive of κεύθω 'hide', in the future sense, as ἐπικεύσω above. The · ends the unit, and the sign itself follows.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κεν δή μοι ξυμβλήμενος ἄλλος ὁδίτης
φήῃ ἀθηρηλοιγὸν ἔχειν ἀνὰ φαιδίμῳ ὤμῳ,
sentences.tr:
hoppote ken dē moi xymblēmenos allos hoditēs
phēēi athērēloigon echein ana phaidimōi ōmōi,
sentences.l:
Whenever indeed, meeting me, another wayfarer
shall say that I have a chaff-ruiner on my glorious shoulder,
sentences.i: When another traveller meets me and says that I am carrying a winnowing-shovel on my glorious shoulder,
sentences.n: ὁππότε κεν δή is 'whenever indeed', with the present subjunctive φήῃ 'shall say' (from φημί). ξυμβλήμενος is the aorist middle participle of συμβάλλω in the old spelling, 'meeting'. ὁδίτης is 'wayfarer'. ἀθηρηλοιγόν is a compound whose first element is disputed; 'chaff-ruiner' is the traditional reading, and the tool meant is a winnowing-shovel, which he will take the oar to be. ἀνὰ φαιδίμῳ ὤμῳ is 'on the glorious shoulder', ἀνά with the dative in the epic way; φαίδιμος keeps its house rendering 'glorious' even of a shoulder.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε μ’ ἐν γαίῃ πήξαντ’ ἐκέλευεν ἐρετμόν,
ἔρξανθ’ ἱερὰ καλὰ Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι,
ἀρνειὸν ταῦρόν τε συῶν τ’ ἐπιβήτορα κάπρον,
sentences.tr:
kai tote m’ en gaiēi pēxant’ ekeleuen eretmon,
erxanth’ hiera kala Poseidaōni anakti,
arneion tauron te syōn t’ epibētora kapron,
sentences.l:
and then me, in the earth fixing the oar, he bade,
offering fine sacrifices to Poseidon the lord,
a ram and a bull and a boar, mounter of sows,
sentences.i: and then he told me, when I had fixed the oar in the ground and made fine sacrifices to lord Poseidon, a ram, a bull, and a boar that mounts sows,
sentences.n: μ’ is με, the accusative of the person bidden: ἐκέλευεν 'he bade' takes it, and the aorist participles πήξαντ’ (πήγνυμι 'fix') and ἔρξανθ’ (ῥέζω 'offer') agree with it: 'he bade me, having fixed … and having offered …, go home', the infinitives of the order coming in the next unit. ἔρξανθ’ is ἔρξαντα with its τ aspirated before the rough breathing of ἱερά. ἱερὰ καλά is 'fine sacrifices', and Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι 'to lord Poseidon'. ἀρνειόν is 'ram', ταῦρον 'bull', and συῶν τ’ ἐπιβήτορα κάπρον 'a boar, the mounter of sows' (συῶν is the genitive plural of σῦς).

sentences.t:
οἴκαδ’ ἀποστείχειν, ἔρδειν θ’ ἱερὰς ἑκατόμβας
ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι,
πᾶσι μάλ’ ἑξείης·
sentences.tr:
oikad’ aposteichein, erdein th’ hieras hekatombas
athanatoisi theoisi, toi ouranon euryn echousi,
pasi mal’ hexeiēs·
sentences.i: to go back home and offer sacred hecatombs to the immortal gods who hold the broad heaven, to every one of them in turn;
sentences.n: οἴκαδ’ ἀποστείχειν is 'to go away home' (οἴκαδε 'homeward'), another infinitive after ἐκέλευεν at 276; ἔρδειν θ’ is 'and to offer', ἔρδω being 'do', used of sacrifice. ἑκατόμβη is a hecatomb, a large sacrifice. ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι is 'to the immortal gods'. τοί is the relative 'who' (the article-form as relative), and οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι 'hold the wide sky'. πᾶσι μάλ’ ἑξείης is 'to all, one after another', ἑξείης meaning 'in order'. The · ends the unit in the middle of line 281.

sentences.t:
θάνατος δέ μοι ἐξ ἁλὸς αὐτῷ
ἀβληχρὸς μάλα τοῖος ἐλεύσεται, ὅς κέ με πέφνῃ
γήρα’ ὕπο λιπαρῷ ἀρημένον·
sentences.tr:
thanatos de moi ex halos autōi
ablēchros mala toios eleusetai, hos ke me pephnēi
gēra’ hypo liparōi arēmenon·
sentences.i: and death will come to me myself from the sea, a very mild one, such as will kill me when I am worn out under a sleek old age;
sentences.n: The prophecy continues. θάνατος … ἐξ ἁλός: ἐξ ἁλός can mean 'from the sea' or 'away from the sea', and the Greek does not decide; the English keeps 'from the sea'. ἀβληχρός 'mild' is a word whose meaning is not known (ancient guesses are 'gentle', 'feeble', 'slow'). τοῖος … ὅς is 'of such a kind as', and πέφνῃ is the aorist subjunctive of an old verb 'slay' that has no present, here with κε. γήρα’ is γήραϊ, the dative of γῆρας, and ὕπο 'under' is accented because it follows its noun; λιπαρός is 'sleek, shining', so the old age is a comfortable one. ἀρημένον is a participle of an old and uncertain verb, agreeing with με; 'worn' follows the traditional gloss.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ λαοὶ
ὄλβιοι ἔσσονται·
sentences.tr:
amphi de laoi
olbioi essontai·
sentences.l:
and around you the peoples
prosperous will be.
sentences.i: and all about you the people will be prosperous.
sentences.n: ἀμφί is the adverb 'around'; λαοί is 'peoples'; ὄλβιοι is 'prosperous' (ὄλβος 'prosperity'); ἔσσονται is the epic form of ἔσονται. The Greek has no pronoun after ἀμφί; the English repeats that of 11.136 (odyssey-052), where Tiresias addresses Odysseus as "you". Here Odysseus retells the prophecy, so the people are prosperous around him. The · ends the unit in the middle of line 284.

sentences.t: τὰ δέ μοι φάτο πάντα τελεῖσθαι.
sentences.tr: ta de moi phato panta teleisthai.
sentences.l: and these things, to me, he said, would all be fulfilled.”
sentences.i: and he said that all of this would be fulfilled for me.”
sentences.n: τά is the pronoun 'these things'. μοι is 'for me'. φάτο is the imperfect middle of φημί, without augment (Attic ἔφατο), 'he said'. τελεῖσθαι is the future infinitive passive of τελέω, 'be fulfilled'. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of the prophecy and of Odysseus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same formula as at 256, with the same English. Penelope answers the prophecy.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ γῆράς γε θεοὶ τελέουσιν ἄρειον,
ἐλπωρή τοι ἔπειτα κακῶν ὑπάλυξιν ἔσεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ei men dē gēras ge theoi teleousin areion,
elpōrē toi epeita kakōn hypalyxin esesthai.
sentences.l:
“If indeed a better old age at least the gods will bring about,
hope for you then there is that there will be an escape from evils.”
sentences.i: “If the gods will indeed bring about a better old age, then there is hope for you that there will be an escape from evils.”
sentences.n: Penelope answers. εἰ μὲν δή is 'if indeed'. γῆράς γε is 'old age at least', γῆρας being the object of τελέουσιν, the uncontracted future of τελέω 'bring about'. ἄρειον is 'better'. ἐλπωρή is 'hope', with ἐστί understood; τοι is σοι 'for you'. κακῶν ὑπάλυξιν is 'an escape from evils', and ἔσεσθαι is the future infinitive of εἰμί, 'that there will be', depending on ἐλπωρή. The closing quotation mark falls here, at the end of the speech.
